new_statements.quote: The common phonological features observed over the sub-dialects of Khengkha consist of a five main vowel system, pitch accent systems, a restricted set of final consonants, and a restricted set of consonant clusters in initials. It is still premature to describe the phonological system and features in detail; this report can only provide first-hand data and a preliminary analysis. The Khengkha phonological system has not been established yet, therefore, I tried to use the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) to record and describe the phonetic appearance in detail.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand statement says Khengkha has a 'pitch accent system' (shared by all its sub-dialects) but explicitly declines to analyse it; no rule for which syllable carries the accent is given. Pitch is transcribed syllable by syllable with Chao numerals throughout the sketch and the 121-page wordlist (e.g. ŋɑ²¹ 'I', ʔo⁴⁴lo²² 'child', jɑː²³ŋʌ²² 'five'); the nearest related descriptions (Michailovsky & Mazaudon 1994 for Kurtoep/Bumthap; Dorji 2022 fn. 3 for Khengkha) point to a high/low register distinction tied to initial consonants, not to a stress-placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author states the phonology has not yet been established and the analysis is preliminary.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms in a wordlist and elicited sentences); dialects sampled: Trongsa, Trong and Wamling (Zhemgang). The statement is a type statement (pitch accent present) rather than a placement rule; it should be catalogued as 'pitch-accent, placement undescribed'.
new_statements.identity_note: Ikeda 2021 describes Khengkha proper (khen1241) from three sub-dialects (Trongsa; Trong and Wamling in Zhemgang), so identity matches. Michailovsky & Mazaudon 1994 (on file) describes Kurtoep (kurt1248) and Bumthap (bumt1240), not Kheng, and must not be attributed to khen1241. Dorji 2022 is Khengkha (Taktse, Trongsa speaker).

sources.quote: The common phonological features observed over the sub-dialects of Khengkha consist of a five main vowel system, pitch accent systems, a restricted set of final consonants, and a restricted set of consonant clusters in initials. It is still premature to describe the phonological system and features in detail; this report can only provide first-hand data and a preliminary analysis. The Khengkha phonological system has not been established yet, therefore, I tried to use the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) to record and describe the phonetic appearance in detail.
sources.note: Sec. 2 Phonology (p. 73) lists 'pitch accent systems' among the common phonological features of all Khengkha sub-dialects, then says it is 'still premature to describe the phonological system and features in detail'; no rule for where the accent/stress falls is given anywhere. Every syllable in the data is transcribed with Chao pitch numerals (e.g. ŋɑ²¹ 'I', mi²¹ 'person', ʔo⁴⁴lo²² 'child'); 2.1-2.3 cover consonants, vowels, diphthongs/codas only. The 49-page text was searched for stress/accent/tone/pitch/prosody: the p. 73 sentence is the only hit.

sources.citation: Dorji, Tenzin. 2022. Case-marking in Khengkha, a language of central Bhutan. Himalayan Linguistics 21(2): 72-104. DOI 10.5070/H921251781
sources.note: Silent on word stress (the only 'stress' hits are pragmatic 'stress that...' and the gloss STR 'stress particle'). Footnote 3, p. 75: "(') indicates a high register tone onset." — implies a high/low register distinction marked as in Dzongkha romanisation, nothing on placement.

sources.note: Matisoff-200 wordlist (Dzongkha/Bumthap/Khengkha/Sharchop) with Chao pitch numerals on every syllable; no prose on stress, accent or tone (searched the 121 pages; the only 'tonal' hit is the Matisoff 1972 title in the abbreviations).

sources.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd & Martine Mazaudon. 1994. Preliminary notes on the languages of the Bumthang group. In Per Kvaerne (ed.), Tibetan Studies: Proceedings of the 6th Seminar of the IATS, Fagernes 1992, vol. 2, 545-557. Oslo: Institute for Comparative Research in Human Culture. halshs-00259369
sources.note: Phonology section is on Kurtoep (kurt1248) with notes on Bumthap proper: 'two tonal registers, high and low, correlated with voicing oppositions in the initial consonant' (p. 546); 'Tone register (high vs low): A high vs low contrast is found on words with nasal or continuant initials...' (p. 547). No Kheng data: Khengke is mentioned only as 'by all reports' mutually intelligible with Kurtoep and Bumthap (p. 545). Nothing on stress. Context for the group only, not a Khengkha description.
